KP 1. Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
1.?
Find the slope $m$ of $y =\sin \left(\pi \left(x^{2} + 2x - 2\right)\right)$ at $x = 1.$
$m=$
$-4\pi$
H
Wed, Aug 5th @ 2:56 PM|Elapsed: 3:11Incorrect

The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(x^{2} +2x - 2\right). \]

Differentiating gives \[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (2x + 2). \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=\cos u \cdot \pi (2x+2)\\[5pt] &=\pi (2x+2)\cos u\\[5pt] &=\pi (2x+2)\cos \left( \pi \left(x^{2} +2x - 2\right) \right). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find

\begin{align} f'(1) & =\pi (2\cdot1+2)\cos \left( \pi \left(1^{2} +2\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\[3pt] & =4\pi \cos(\pi) \\[3pt] &= 4\pi \cdot (-1) \\[3pt] &= -4\pi \end{align}

Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is \[ m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-4\pi}. \]

Your Answer:
$4\pi$
2.?

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = \cos (5x-2 )$ at the point $\left(\dfrac 2 5,1\right).$

H
Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:03 PM|Elapsed: 6:03Correct

The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=\dfrac 2 5$ is given by $f'\left(\dfrac 2 5\right).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ y = \cos{u}, \qquad u = 5x-2. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = -\sin u \qquad \style{font-family:inherit;}{\text{and}} \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 5. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=-\sin u \cdot 5\\[5pt] &=-5\sin u\\[5pt] &= -5\sin\left(5x-2 \right). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=\dfrac 25,$ we find

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ m=f'\left(\dfrac 25\right) & =- 5 \sin \left(5\cdot \dfrac 2 5-2\right)\\[5pt] & =- 5 \sin 0\\[5pt] &= 0. } \end{eqnarray} Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $\left(\dfrac 2 5,1\right) \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\[5pt] y-1&=0\left(x-\dfrac{2}{5}\right)\\[5pt] y-1&=0\\[5pt] y&=1. \end{align*}

3.?

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $f(x) = \cos{\left(x^3\right)}$ at the point $\left(0,1\right).$

H
Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:05 PM|Elapsed: 1:18Correct

First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 0$ is given by $f'(0).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ y = \cos{u}, \qquad u = x^3. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = -\sin{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =3x^2. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &= -\sin{u} \cdot 3x^2\\[5pt] &=-3x^2\sin(x^3). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find \begin{align} m=f'(0) & = -3(0)^2\sin(0^3) = 0. \end{align}

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(0,1) \mathbin{:}$ \begin{align} y - y_1 & = m(x - x_1)\\[3pt] y - 1 & = 0 \cdot \left(x - 0 \right)\\[3pt] y - 1 & = 0\\[3pt] y & =1. \end{align}

4.?

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=\sec(3x)-2x$ at the point $\left(0,1\right).$

H
Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:07 PM|Elapsed: 2:22Correct

Let $g(x)=\sec(3x )$ and $h(x)=-2x.$ Then,

\begin{align} f(x)&=g(x)+h(x) . \end{align}

First, we differentiate $g(x).$ We express $g(x)=\sec(3x)$ as the composite function \[ g = \sec u, \qquad u = 3x. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d g}{\textrm d u} = \sec u \tan u \qquad \text{and} \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm d x} = 3. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and we get \[ \eqalign{ \require{cancel} \dfrac{\textrm{d}g}{\textrm{d}x}&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}g}{\textrm{d}u}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}\\[5pt] &=\sec u \tan u \cdot (3)\\[5pt] &=3 \sec u \tan u\\[5pt] & =3\sec (3x) \tan (3x) } \]

Next, we differentiate $h(x)=-2x.$

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d h}{\textrm d x} = -2 \]

Hence, \[f'(x)=g'(x)+h'(x)=3\sec (3x) \tan (3x) -2.\]

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find

\begin{align*} m=f'(0) & =3\sec\left(3\cdot 0\right)\tan\left(3\cdot 0\right) -2\\[3pt] & =3\sec 0\tan 0 -2\\[3pt] & =3\cdot 1\cdot 0 - 2\\[3pt] &=-2. \end{align*}

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(0,1) \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} y-y_1&=m(x-x_1)\\[3pt] y-1&=-2 \left(x-0 \right)\\[3pt] y-1&=-2x\\[3pt] y&=-2x+1. \end{align}

5.?
Find the slope $m$ of $f(x) = \sec\left(\pi x^{2}\right)$ at $x = \dfrac{1}{2}.$
$m=$
$\pi\sqrt{2}$
M
Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:09 PM|Elapsed: 1:09Incorrect

First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ is given by $f'\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. We express $f(x)$ as the composite function \[ f = \sec{u}, \qquad u = \pi x^{2}. \]

Differentiating gives \[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = \sec{u}\tan{u}, \qquad\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 2\pi x. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} & = \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &= \sec{u}\tan{u} \cdot 2\pi x \\[5pt] &= 2\pi x \sec{\left(\pi x^{2}\right)}\tan{\left(\pi x^{2}\right)}. \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, we find \begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ f'\left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right) &= 2\pi \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot \sec{\left[\pi\cdot\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]}\tan{\left[\pi\cdot\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}\right]} \\[5pt] &= \pi \sec{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)} \tan{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)} \\[5pt] &= \pi \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= \pi\sqrt{2}.} \end{eqnarray}

Therefore, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$ is $\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\pi\sqrt{2}}.$

Your Answer:
$\pi$

Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:11 PM|Elapsed: 1:34Correct

First, we express $y$ as the composite function

\[ y = 8\csc{u}, \qquad u = 10x \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = -8\csc u \cot u \qquad \style{font-family:inherit;}{\text{and}} \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 10. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

7.?

Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=\cot\left(1-\dfrac x 5 \right)$ at the point where $x =1.$

M
Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:12 PM|Elapsed: 1:43Incorrect

The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ f = \cot{u}, \qquad u = 1-\dfrac x 5. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = -\csc^2 u \qquad \text{and}\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -\dfrac{1}{5}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=-\csc^2 u \cdot \left( -\dfrac{1}{5}\right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{5}\csc^2 \left(1-\dfrac{x}{5}\right). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ f'(x) & =\dfrac 1 5\csc^2\left(1-\dfrac 1 5 \right) \\[3pt] & =\dfrac 1 5\csc^2\left(\dfrac 4 5 \right) . } \end{eqnarray} Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is $\dfrac{1}{5}\csc^2\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right).$

Your Answer:
$-\dfrac 1 5\csc^2\left(\dfrac 4 5 \right)$
8.?
Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $f(x) = \csc{\left(\dfrac{\pi x^{3}}{6}\right)}$ at the point $(1,2).$

$-\pi\sqrt{3}$
$x \: + \:$
$\pi\sqrt{3}+2$
H
Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:34 PM|Elapsed: 21:06Correct

First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function \[ f = \csc{u}, \qquad u = \dfrac{\pi x^{3}}{6}. \]

Differentiating gives \[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = -\csc{u}\cot{u} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} x^{2}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=\left(-\csc{u}\cot{u}\right) \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{2} x^{2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{\pi}{2} x^{2} \csc{\left(\dfrac{\pi x^{3}}{6}\right)\cot{\left(\dfrac{\pi x^{3}}{6}\right)}}. \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find \begin{align} m=f'(1)& =-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \cdot 1^2 \cdot \csc{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\cot{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)}} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot \sqrt{3} \\[5pt] & = -\pi\sqrt{3}. \end{align}

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $\left(1,2\right) \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\[5pt] y-2 &= -\pi\sqrt{3}(x-1)\\[5pt] y &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\pi\sqrt{3}}x + \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\pi\sqrt{3} + 2} \end{align*}

Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:36 PM|Elapsed: 1:15Correct

First, we express \[ f(x) = (\cos{(x)})^{7}. \]

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function \[ f = u^{7}, \qquad u = \cos{(x)}. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm d u} = 7u^6, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -\sin{(x)}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get \begin{align*} f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &= 7u^6 \cdot (-\sin{(x)})\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-7\cos^6{(x)}\sin{(x)}}. \end{align*}

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm df}{\textrm d u} = -6u^2, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \cos{(x)}. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

12.?

Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y =\cos \left(\sin x \right)$ at the point $\left(0,1 \right).$

H
Wed, Aug 5th @ 3:39 PM|Elapsed: 1:01Correct

First, the slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 0$ is given by $f'(0).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[ f = \cos{u}, \qquad u = \sin x. \]

Differentiating gives

\[ \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = -\sin{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =\cos x. \]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x} &= \dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt] &=-\sin u \cdot (\cos x)\\[5pt] &=-\cos x \sin (\sin x). \end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=0,$ we find \[ \eqalign{ f'(0)&=-\cos (0) \sin (\sin (0))\\[3pt] &=-1 \cdot 0 \\[3pt] &=0. } \]

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(0,1) \mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} y-y_1 &= m(x-x_1)\\[3pt] y-1 &= (0)\cdot\left(x-0\right)\\[3pt] y&=1. \end{align}
